source_text: Primo quidem oblivionis capacem animam non cedam, quia tantam illi concessit divinitatem, ut Deo adaequetur: innatam eam facit, quod et solum armare potuissem ad testimonium plenae divinitatis: adjicit immortalem, incorruptibilem, incorporalem, quia hoc et Deum credidit, invisibilem, ineffigiabilem, uniformem, principalem, rationalem, intellectualem. Quid amplius proscriberet animam, si eam Deum nuncuparet? Nos autem qui nihil Deo appendimus, hoc ipso animam longe infra Deum expendimus, quod natam eam agnoscimus, ac per hoc dilutioris divinitatis, et exilioris felicitatis; ut flatum, non ut spiritum; et si immortalem, ut hoc sit divinitatis, tamen passibilem, ut hoc sit nativitatis: ideoque et a primordio exorbitationis capacem, et inde etiam oblivionis affinem. Satis de isto cum Hermogene. Caeterum, quae, ut haberi merito possit ex peraequatione omnium proprietatum deus, nulli passioni subjacebit; ita nec oblivioni, cum tanta sit injuria oblivio, quanta est gloria ejus, cujus injuria est, memoria scilicet: quam et ipse Plato sensuum et intellectuum salutem, et Cicero thesaurum omnium studiorum praedicavit. Nec hoc jam in dubium deducetur, an tam divina anima memoriam potuerit amittere; sed an quam amiserit, recuperare denuo possit. Quae enim non debuit oblivisci, si oblita sit, nescio an valeat recordari. Ita utrumque meae animae, non platonicae congruet. Secundo gradu opponam: natura compotem animam facis idearum illarum, annon? Imo natura, inquis. Nemo ergo concedet naturalem scientiam naturalium excidere artium. Excidet studiorum, excidet doctrinarum, disciplinarum, excidet fortasse et ingeniorum, et affectuum: quae naturae videntur, non tamen sunt, quia, ut praemisimus et pro locis, et pro institutionibus, et pro corpulentiis, ac valetudinibus, et pro potestatibus dominatricibus, pro libertatibus arbitrii, ex accidentibus constant. Naturalium vero scientia ne in bestiis quidem deficit. Plane obliviscetur feritatis leo, mansuetudinis eruditione praeventus, et cum toto suggestu jubarum, delicium fiet Berenices alicujus reginae, lingua genas ejus emaculans; mores bestiam relinquent: scientia naturalium permanebit. Non obliviscetur idem naturalium pabulorum, naturalium remediorum, naturalium terrorum; etsi de piscibus, etsi de placentis regina ei obtulerit, carnem desiderabit; etsi languenti theriacam composuerit, simiam leo requiret: et si nullum illi venabulum obfirmabit, gallum tamen formidabit. Perinde et homini omnium forsitan obliviosissimo inobliterata perseverabit sola scientia naturalium, ut sola scilicet naturalis; memor semper manducandi in esurie, et bibendi in siti, et oculis videndum, et auribus audiendum, et naribus odorandum, et ore gustandum, et manu contrectandum. Hi sunt certe sensus, quos philosophia depretiat intellectualium praelatione. Igitur si naturalis scientia sensualium permanet, quomodo intellectualium, quae potior habetur, intercidit? Unde nunc ipsa vis oblivionis antecedentis recordationem? Ex multitudine, ait, temporis. Satis improspecte. Quantitas enim temporis non pertinebit ad eam rem quae innata dicatur, ac per hoc potissimum aeterna credatur. Quod enim aeternum est, eo quia et innatum est, neque initium, neque finem temporis admittendo, nullum modum temporis patitur; cui temporis modus nullus est, nec ulla demutatione tempori subest, nec ea de multitudine tempori vis est. Si tempus in caussa est oblivionis, cur, ex quo anima corpori inducitur, memoria delabitur, quasi exinde tempus anima sustineat, quae sine dubio prior corpore, non fuit utique sine tempore? Ingressa vero corpus, statimne obliviscitur, an aliquanto post? Si statim, et quae erit temporis nondum supputandi multitudo? infantia scilicet. Si aliquando post, ergo illo in spatio ante tempora oblivionis memor adhuc aget anima, et quale est, ut postea obliviscatur, et rursus postea recordetur? Quoquo autem tempore illam oblivio irruerit, quantus hic etiam habebitur modus temporis? tota opinor vitae decursio satis non erit ad evertendam memoriam tanti ante corpus aevi. Sed rursus Plato caussam demutat in corpus. Quasi et hoc fide dignum, ut nata substantia innatae vim exstinguat. Magnae autem et multae differentiae corporum, pro gentilitate, pro magnitudine, pro habitudine, pro aetate, pro valetudine. Num ergo et oblivionum differentiae aestimabuntur? Sed uniformis oblivio est; ergo non erit corporalitas multiformis in caussa exitus uniformis. Multa item documenta, teste ipso Platone, divinationem animae probaverunt, quae proposuimus jam Hermogeni. Sed nec quisquam hominum, non et ipse aliquando praesagam animam suam sentit, aut ominis, aut periculi, aut gaudii augurem. Si divinationi non obstrepit corpus, nec memoriae, opinor, officiet. In eodem certe corpore, et obliviscuntur animae, et recordantur. Si qua corporis ratio incutit oblivionem, quomodo contrariam ejus admittet recordationem? quia et ipsa post oblivionem recordatio, memoria recidiva est. Quod primae memoriae adversatur, cur non et secundae refragatur? Postremo, qui magis reminiscerentur quam pueruli, ut recentiores animae, ut nondum immersae domesticis ac publicis curis, ut ipsis solis deditae studiis, quorum discentiae reminiscentiae fiunt? Imo cur non ex aequo omnes recordamur, cum ex aequo omnes obliviscamur, sed tantummodo Philosophi? Ne hi quidem omnes. Plato scilicet solus in tanta gentium sylva, in tanto sapientium prato, idearum et oblitus et recordatus est. Igitur si nullo modo consistit argumentatio ista praecipua, totum illud pariter eversum est, cui accommodata est, ut animae et innatae, et in coelestibus conversatae, et consciae divinorum illic, et inde delatae, et hic recordatae crederentur, ad occasiones plane haereticis subministrandas.
pass_a_gloss: First indeed I will not concede that the soul is capable of oblivion, because so much divinity has been granted to it, that it is equal to God: it makes it innate, which I could have used alone as testimony to full divinity: it adds that it is immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal, because it is believed to be God, invisible, ineffable, uniform, principal, rational, intellectual. What more would it prescribe for the soul, if it were to call it God? But we, who attribute nothing to God, by this very fact estimate the soul to be far inferior to God, because we recognize it as born, and therefore of a more diluted divinity, and of a more meager happiness; like a breath, not like a spirit; and if immortal, so that it may be of divinity, yet passible, so that it may be of birth: and therefore also capable of error from the beginning, and from there also akin to oblivion. Enough about this with Hermogenes. Moreover, what can be considered a god from the equality of all properties, will not be subject to any passion; thus not to oblivion, since oblivion is as great an injury as the glory of the one whose injury it is, namely memory: which even Plato and Cicero have proclaimed to be the salvation of the senses and intellect, and the treasure of all studies. Nor will it be doubted now whether such a divine soul could have lost memory; but whether, if it has lost it, it can recover it again. For what it should not have forgotten, if it has forgotten, I do not know if it can recall. Thus both will be fitting for my soul, not the Platonic one. Secondly, I will oppose: you make the soul capable of those ideas by nature, do you not? Indeed, by nature, you say. Therefore, no one will concede that natural knowledge of natural things can fall away. It will fall away from studies, from doctrines, from disciplines, it will perhaps fall away from talents and affections: which seem to be of nature, but are not, because, as we have said before, they consist of accidents, and of institutions, and of bodily conditions, and of health, and of dominant powers, and of freedoms of the will. But the knowledge of natural things does not even fail in beasts. Clearly, a lion will forget its ferocity, having been prevented by training, and with all its pride, it will become the delight of some queen Berenice, its tongue licking her cheeks; it will leave behind its beastly ways: the knowledge of natural things will remain. The same lion will not forget its natural food, its natural remedies, its natural terrors; even if it is offered fish or royal delicacies, it will desire flesh; even if a remedy is composed for it when it is sick, it will seek a monkey: and if no hunting spear is presented to it, it will still fear a rooster. Similarly, in man, perhaps the most forgetful of all, the knowledge of natural things will remain unobliterated, as the only natural thing; always mindful of eating when hungry, and drinking when thirsty, and seeing with the eyes, and hearing with the ears, and smelling with the nose, and tasting with the mouth, and touching with the hand. These are certainly the senses, which philosophy devalues in favor of intellectual things. Therefore, if natural knowledge of sensual things remains, how can intellectual knowledge, which is considered superior, fall away? Whence now comes the power of oblivion preceding recollection? From the multitude of time, it is said. This is not well considered. For the quantity of time does not pertain to that which is said to be innate, and therefore is believed to be eternal. For what is eternal, because it is also innate, does not admit a beginning or end of time, and does not suffer any mode of time; to which no mode of time is, and no change of time is subject, and no power of time is. If time is the cause of oblivion, why, from the time the soul is introduced into the body, does memory slip away, as if the soul, which was certainly prior to the body, did not exist without time? Indeed, when it enters the body, does it immediately forget, or after some time? If immediately, what will be the multitude of time not yet reckoned? Clearly, infancy. If after some time, then in that space before the times of oblivion, the soul will still be mindful, and what kind of thing is it, that it later forgets, and again later recalls? By whatever time oblivion may come, what mode of time will be had? I think the whole course of life will not be enough to overturn the memory of so much time before the body. But again, Plato changes the cause to the body. As if this too were worthy of faith, that a born substance extinguishes the power of an innate one. There are indeed great and many differences of bodies, according to nation, size, condition, age, health. Will the differences of oblivion therefore be estimated? But oblivion is uniform; therefore, the multiformity of the body will not be the cause of the uniform exit. Many proofs, with Plato himself as witness, have demonstrated the divination of the soul, which we have already proposed to Hermogenes. But no one of men, not even Plato himself, sometimes feels his soul to be a predictor of things to come, or an omen, or a warning of danger, or a sign of joy. If the body does not hinder divination, I think it will not hinder memory either. In the same body, souls both forget and recall. If some reason of the body incites oblivion, how will it admit the contrary recollection? Because even recollection after oblivion is a renewed memory. What contradicts the first memory, why does it not also contradict the second? Finally, who would recall more than children, as more recent souls, not yet immersed in domestic and public cares, but dedicated solely to studies, whose learning becomes recollections? Why do we not all recall equally, since we all forget equally, but only the philosophers? Not even all of them. Clearly, Plato alone, in such a great multitude of nations, in such a great field of wise men, was both forgetful and mindful of ideas. Therefore, if this principal argument does not hold in any way, the whole thing, to which it was accommodated, is equally overturned, so that it was believed that souls are both innate and conversant in heavenly things, and conscious of divine things there, and thence transferred, and here recalled, to provide occasions for heretics.
pass_b_english: I will not concede that the soul is capable of oblivion. The divinity granted to it is so great that it makes the soul equal to God. That alone — its innateness — would have been enough to testify to its full divinity. On top of that, it is said to be immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal, invisible, ineffable, uniform, principal, rational, intellectual — attributes believed to belong to God. What more could you prescribe for the soul if you were to call it God outright? We, however, attribute nothing to God. Therefore, we estimate the soul to be far inferior to God, because we recognize it as born. Its divinity is therefore diluted, its happiness meager. It is like a breath, not a spirit. Even if it is immortal, that immortality serves its divinity; but it is passible, and that passibility serves its birth. Consequently, it was capable of error from the beginning, and from there also akin to oblivion. That is enough on this point with Hermogenes.

Moreover, whatever can be considered a god by the equality of all divine properties will not be subject to any passion. Thus, it will not be subject to oblivion either, since oblivion is as great an injury as the glory of the one whose injury it is — namely, memory. Plato himself proclaimed memory the salvation of the senses and intellect, and Cicero called it the treasure of all studies. The question now is not whether such a divine soul could have lost memory, but whether, once lost, it can recover it again. For what it should not have forgotten, if it has forgotten, I do not know if it can recall. So both oblivion and recovery fit my soul, not the Platonic one.

Second, I will oppose you on this: you claim the soul is capable of those ideas by nature, do you not? "Indeed, by nature," you say. Then no one will concede that natural knowledge of natural things can fall away. Knowledge of studies, doctrines, disciplines may fall away. Perhaps talents and affections fall away too. These seem natural but are not, because they consist of accidents — institutions, bodily conditions, health, dominant powers, freedoms of the will. But the knowledge of natural things does not even fail in beasts. A lion will forget its ferocity when prevented by training, and with all its pride intact it will become the delight of some queen Berenice, licking her cheeks with its tongue. It will leave behind its beastly ways, yet the knowledge of natural things will remain. That same lion will not forget its natural food, its natural remedies, its natural terrors. Even if offered fish or royal delicacies, it will desire flesh. Even if a remedy is composed for it when sick, it will seek a monkey. And if no hunting spear is presented, it will still fear a rooster. Similarly, in man — perhaps the most forgetful of all — the knowledge of natural things will remain unobliterated, as the only truly natural thing. He will always be mindful of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, smelling with the nose, tasting with the mouth, touching with the hand. These are the senses that philosophy devalues in favor of intellectual things. Therefore, if natural knowledge of sensual things remains, how can intellectual knowledge — considered superior — fall away?

Where, then, does the power of oblivion preceding recollection come from? "From the multitude of time," it is said. That is not well considered. The quantity of time does not pertain to what is said to be innate, and therefore believed to be eternal. What is eternal, because it is innate, admits neither beginning nor end of time, and suffers no mode of time. To what has no mode of time, no change of time applies, and no power of time belongs. If time is the cause of oblivion, why does memory slip away from the moment the soul is introduced into the body — as if the soul, certainly prior to the body, did not exist without time? Once it enters the body, does it immediately forget, or after some time? If immediately, what multitude of time — not yet reckoned — would there be? Clearly, infancy. If after some time, then in that space before the times of oblivion the soul would still be mindful. What kind of thing is it, that it later forgets, and then later recalls again? Whenever oblivion may strike, what mode of time would be involved? I think the whole course of life will not be enough to overturn the memory of so much time before the body.

But again, Plato shifts the cause to the body. As if this too were worthy of faith — that a born substance extinguishes the power of an innate one. There are great and many differences among bodies — by nation, size, condition, age, health. Will the differences of oblivion therefore be estimated? But oblivion is uniform. Therefore, the multiformity of the body cannot be the cause of a uniform exit. Many proofs, with Plato himself as witness, have demonstrated the soul's divination, which we have already proposed to Hermogenes. Not a single human being fails to sometimes feel his own soul as a predictor of things to come — an omen, a warning of danger, a sign of joy. If the body does not hinder divination, I think it will not hinder memory either. In the same body, souls both forget and recall. If some reason of the body incites oblivion, how will it admit the contrary recollection? Recollection after oblivion is a renewed memory. What contradicts the first memory — why does it not also contradict the second? Finally, who would recall more than children — as more recent souls, not yet immersed in domestic and public cares, dedicated solely to studies whose learning becomes recollections? Why do we not all recall equally, since we all forget equally — but only the philosophers? Not even all of them. Clearly, Plato alone, in such a vast multitude of nations, in such a vast field of wise men, was both forgetful and mindful of the ideas. Therefore, if this principal argument does not hold in any way, the whole structure to which it was accommodated is equally overturned — the belief that souls are innate, conversant in heavenly things, conscious of divine things there, thence transferred, and here recalled — providing occasions plainly for heretics.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological and philosophical arguments of Tertullian. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Latin (e.g., the distinction between 'breath' and 'spirit' for 'flatum' and 'spiritum', and the causal relations regarding divinity and birth). Pass B maintains the fidelity of Pass A while providing a fluent English reading. All clauses, including the specific list of divine attributes and the biological/natural examples, are accounted for. Scripture/citations: No specific biblical verses were quoted in the text, though the text alludes to philosophical concepts. The title 'The Soul's Capacity for Oblivion' correctly names the thought.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key terms. The inline citations match the content, and the translation adheres to the source text without adding or omitting content. The title accurately represents the content of the passage.
